Approach step 1 says the alarms use 'metric math / dimensions'. Cache-ratio math by definition needs a cache-read token series, and unit-cost math needs output tokens.

Retrieved: AWS Bedrock runtime-metrics docs (docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring-runtime-metrics.html) say 'ModelId – all metrics'. findings.finding: The plan never checks that AWS/Bedrock publishes the cache and output token series these alarms depend on for the 5.5 inference-profile ModelIds. AC2's live check covers only Invocations and InputTokenCount. A cache-ratio alarm needs CacheReadInputTokenCount, and a unit-cost alarm needs OutputTokenCount (and the cache series too). If either series is absent or empty for an inference-profile id, metric math that treats missing data as not breaching would stay OK forever. That is the same 'can never fire' failure this bug is fixing.

scenarios: CacheReadInputTokenCount is not emitted (or is always zero) under the us.anthropic.*-5-5 profile id, so the cache-ratio alarm sits in OK or INSUFFICIENT_DATA and never fires.
OutputTokenCount is missing for a model id, so the unit-cost expression understates cost and never crosses its threshold.

The stated defect is alarms that 'can never fire' because they watch metrics with no data. INSUFFICIENT_DATA is how that looks for an alarm that does not treat missing data as OK.
findings.finding: AC2's verification is weak in three ways. (a) 'ERROR' is not a CloudWatch alarm state; the states are OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA. (b) Accepting INSUFFICIENT_DATA admits exactly the original failure mode: an alarm whose query matches no data. (c) Checking Invocations and InputTokenCount for each ModelId does not prove each alarm's own metric or metric-math query returns data. The cache-ratio alarm likely depends on cache-token metrics, and the unit-cost alarm may use a custom namespace or other dimensions.

findings.finding: The proposed check can't tell a working alarm from one that can never fire, which is the same failure this bug reports. The broken 4.x alarms showed state OK for two months while watching dead ids, so 'OK or INSUFFICIENT_DATA' says nothing about whether an alarm works. The extra get-metric-data check only covers Invocations and InputTokenCount. The cache-ratio math (cache / inp) and the unit-cost math also use CacheReadInputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount, with no FILL. With treat_missing_data=notBreaching, a missing cache series makes the expression return nothing, and that counts as not breaching. That happens in exactly the case the cache-ratio alarm exists for: cache reads dropping to zero. So the alarm can be blind to its main target, and the plan's verification wouldn't catch it.
scenarios: A caching regression stops all cache reads. If Bedrock doesn't publish the CacheReadInputTokenCount series for those hours, `cache / inp` returns nothing, notBreaching applies, and the alarm stays OK during the incident it was built to catch.

OutputTokenCount or CacheReadInputTokenCount isn't published under the inference-profile ModelId. AC2 still passes because it only checks Invocations and InputTokenCount, but the unit-cost expression never evaluates.
findings.suggested_fix: In AC2, replace the raw-metric check with: 'aws cloudwatch get-metric-data using each alarm's exact metric_query set (from describe-alarms Metrics) over the last 24h returns non-empty values for the return_data expression, and CacheReadInputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, InputTokenCount and Invocations are each non-empty for every referenced ModelId.' In step 2, wrap the cache series as FILL(cache,0) in the ratio expression so a total loss of cache reads counts as breaching, not missing.

The Terraform-managed client-error alarm in infra/terraform/monitoring_eb6e.tf still hard-codes 6 ModelId literals, and both alarm sets have to match REBAR_LLM_*_MODEL by hand. The underlying cause of this bug is alarm model ids silently drifting from the configured models. This plan adds a second independent copy of those ids instead of a single source, so the next model move needs coordinated edits in several places and can go stale the same way. A better option: one shared Terraform local or variable for the model classes and their ids that both monitoring_eb6e.tf and the new alarms use, plus a `make verify` check that those ids match the REBAR_LLM_*_MODEL defaults.
findings.location: Approach step 2 ('keyed so a future model move is a one-line change')
scenarios: The next model move (e.g. to 6.x) updates the new cost-alarm local but misses the six literals in monitoring_eb6e.tf, or the other way round, so one alarm family watches dead ids again.
